sec.title: Background
sec.p: Telemedicine interventions (TMIs) for heart failure (HF) can reduce hospitalizations and deaths. It is unclear if low literacy and limited access to technology in low‐ and middle‐income countries affect these benefits. We evaluated whether TMIs added to usual care could reduce HF‐related rehospitalizations in patients discharged from hospitals in Brazil.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A randomized clinical trial was conducted in 6 public hospitals from September 2021 to June 2022. Patients hospitalized because of HF were randomized to usual care or a multicomponent TMIs. The TMI included weekly nurse‐led structured telephone support to monitor weight, blood pressure, heart rate, decompensation signs, and treatment adherence, while promoting self‐care education, including diuretic dose adjustments. The nurse was linked to a cardiologist for teleconsultations, according to predefined decision trees. An educational program via text messages was also provided. The primary outcome was HF‐related rehospitalizations at 180 days, analyzed by intention‐to‐treat analysis.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Of 127 randomized patients (TMI, n=70; usual care, n=57), mean±SD age was 64±11 years, 48% were women, 71% were Black race, 33% had <4 years of education, 65% were New York Heart Association class III/IV, and 68% had reduced ejection fraction (≤50%). At 180 days, 26% of the TMI group had HF‐related rehospitalizations versus 46% in usual care (relative risk [RR]=0.56, P<0.02). All‐cause death or rehospitalizations occurred in 30% of the TMI group versus 47% in usual care (RR=0.63, P=0.04). Results were consistent in “per‐protocol” and subgroup analyses. Enrollment was lower than expected because of COVID‐19 disruptions.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: TMI reduced HF‐related rehospitalizations, demonstrating its potential to improve clinical outcomes in this population.

list-item.p: In this randomized clinical trial that included 127 adults in Brazil, a middle‐income country, a telemedicine intervention based on weekly structured telephone support by a nurse manager linked to a cardiologist plus a remote educational program significantly reduced heart failure rehospitalizations by 44%.
Telemedicine interventions in postdischarge care are effective strategies to reduce heart failure rehospitalizations in low‐ and middle‐income countries.
Telemedicine interventions should be considered in the management of postdischarge patients with heart failure in low‐ and middle‐income countries to improve clinical outcomes.

Further work, including cost‐effectiveness evaluation and implementation studies, is necessary to better understand the benefits and limits of this telemedicine intervention in the low‐ and middle‐income country context.

body.p: Cardiovascular diseases are the main cause of death in many low‐ and middle‐income countries (LMICs), including Brazil. 1 Heart failure (HF) accounted for 40% of cardiovascular disease hospitalizations from 2008 to 2021 in the country. 1 Readmission rates for HF are high, with recent studies showing >30% of rehospitalizations within 90 days of discharge, being these readmissions related to worse clinical outcomes and costs. 2 , 3 , 4

As such, the transition of care from hospital to home is a critical period to prevent rehospitalizations, 3 which have been related to the following barriers: (1) poor communication of discharge plans; (2) patients' insufficient knowledge about HF; and (3) inadequate access to early care, particularly to cardiologists. 5 , 6 , 7 Taken together, this unfavorable context impairs patients' self‐care, adherence to life‐saving medications, and identification of early decompensation; and it also delays guideline‐directed medical therapy (GDMT) optimization, which are underused and can reduce HF hospitalizations. 8 , 9 , 10

By attempting to address these barriers, telemedicine interventions (TMIs) may contribute to reducing HF‐related rehospitalizations. 11 , 12 , 13 In a recent meta‐analysis that compared TMI with standard of care, a 22% reduction in first HF hospitalizations (pooled incidence rate ratio, 0.78 [95% CI, 0.70–0.86]; I 2: 26%) with TMI was observed, although with moderate heterogeneity. 14 However, it is unknown whether these clinical benefits remain in LMICs, where lower education and digital literacy are present. 15 , 16 , 17 We aim to evaluate whether a multicomponent TMI added to usual care would reduce HF‐related rehospitalizations in the public health system in Brazil.

sec.title: METHODS
sec.p: Data will be available on evaluation of the requests by the study leadership.

sec.title: Study Design and Setting
sec.p: This randomized, controlled, multicenter clinical trial, with 2 parallel arms and allocation ratio 1:1, was designed to test if a multicomponent TMI could reduce rehospitalizations for HF compared with usual care in the Brazilian public health system (Sistema Único de Sáude). The Sistema Único de Sáude has universal coverage, although hospitalizations in public hospitals are more frequent among the more socially vulnerable population, who do not have private insurance. 18 , 19 HF usual care is not standardized in the Sistema Único de Sáude, and can occur in primary health care centers and/or by cardiologist in specialized centers. Some GDMT classes are available to all patients with HF free of charge, including angiotensin‐converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, β‐blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists. Angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitor and sodium‐glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors are not available free of charge and are high‐cost medications in Brazil. This trial was conducted in 6 public hospitals that comprised 73% of all HF hospitalization in Belo Horizonte, the capital city of Minas Gerais state (2.3 million inhabitants), from September 2021 to June 2022. 20 , 21 This trial is 1 of a 3‐arm study to evaluate TMI for chronic conditions in Brazil. The trial protocol (HF arm, Data S1) was approved by institutional review boards at participating sites, and the HF arm protocol has been published in detail. 22 The reporting of the results of this trial adheres to the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials guideline. 23

sec.title: Randomization
sec.p: Simple randomization occurring within each site‐based stratum, no more than 48 hours before participants' discharge, was applied by research assistants. 22 A centralized, web‐based automated randomization system was used to conceal allocation. The study was only blinded for outcome assessments, because of the nature of the intervention.

sec.title: Participants
sec.p: All patients hospitalized for HF (International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision [ICD‐10], code I50.0) at the 6 inclusion sites were screened for eligibility. Inclusion criteria were as follows: patients living in Belo Horizonte, aged >30 years, using diuretics before admission or on hospital discharge. Patients were excluded if: life expectancy <6 months for other reasons; in renal replacement therapy; pregnant; unable to complete the interview or use the devices (blood pressure cuff and scale); had cognitive alterations with no responsible caregiver; illiterate with no responsible caregiver; had a condition that could limit the conformity with the study procedures (ie, known drug abuse); hospitalization was attributable to acute HF causes (eg, acute coronary syndromes, cardiac surgeries, or device implantation); had planned invasive procedures in 30 days; were on the waiting list for heart transplantation or had a left ventricular assist device; or were participating in other HF intervention studies. Smartphone or data package could be supplied to the participant or caregiver, if needed. Eligible patients were invited to participate and received an educational booklet about HF self‐care on invitation. If patients agreed to participate, they signed the informed consent before being submitted to study procedures. The participants' flow is in Data S2.

sec.title: Intervention
sec.p: The multicomponent TMI included was implemented by a nurse case manager who was assigned for every participant and met the participant once at a visit in the research center, up to 7 days after hospital discharge. In this first visit, the case manager provided blood pressure cuff and scale to participants, and educated them about the study's daily logs for vital signs, subjective health status assessment, and medication use registration. After this first visit, the intervention was remote until 180±15 days.

The TMI provided the participant a structured telephone support (STS) program, a self‐care educational remote program (consisting of twice a week unidirectional semipersonalized text messages, as in Data S3), and a 2‐way channel for questions through text messages to the case manager, during working hours. The case managers were linked to a cardiologist who was activated for teleconsultations, according to predefined clinical decision trees based on clinical status and alarm signs. 8 The case manager contacted the participant weekly (or biweekly, if in New York Heart Association [NYHA] class I or II, no hospitalization or medication change in the past month, and no alarm signs) for a STS to evaluate the following: (1) the daily monitoring of weight, blood pressure, and heart rate collected by patients, (2) to assess decompensation signs and symptoms, (3) to address treatment adherence barriers, and (4) to promote self‐care education, including adjustments of diuretic dosing. At the end of the STS call, the participant was assigned to a management pathway based on the presence of alarm signs and current NYHA class. Briefly, there were 5 pathways that included: (1) referral to emergency evaluation, (2) cardiology teleconsultation in the same day, (3) elective cardiology teleconsultation (up to 7 days), (4) diuretic dose adjustment supported by the case manager, and according to a protocol designed for this study, or (5) maintenance (Data S4). The decision trees were embedded in a management system software developed at the Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais. Participants were encouraged to participate with daily collection and recording of vital signs and weight in the study logs, and by classifying their daily health status. The rationale of this classification was to inform the case manager about change in HF symptoms, and to promote self‐knowledge.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: The primary outcome was HF‐related rehospitalizations, evaluated by an independent adjudication committee composed of a nurse and a cardiologist. Secondary outcomes included all‐cause death; all‐cause and HF rehospitalization; and emergency health services admissions. Outcomes were collected through telephone or video calls at 180±15 days after randomization by 2 independent research assistants, with confirmatory documents sent by text messages. Alternatively, deaths and hospitalizations up to 180 days after participant's randomization were informed by Belo Horizonte's health secretariat administrative database, the source for the national databases, which has been rated as having good quality, 24 as prespecified in the trial protocol. 22

sec.title: Sample Size
sec.p: Considering a rehospitalization rate of 0.39 in the control and 0.26 in the intervention group from a previous STS study in Brazil, 25 80% power, a 2‐sided type I error of 0.05, and estimated loss to follow‐up of 25%, our calculated sample size was 340 participants.

sec.title: Qualitative Analysis
sec.p: At the end of the trial, the last 10 participants from each group were invited to participate in the qualitative phase to share their personal experiences within the study. Two focus groups were conducted, one with 5 participants and 1 caregiver from the intervention group and other with 4 participants and 1 caregiver from the control group. More detailed methods following the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research guidelines, and the sociodemographic characteristics of the participants are shown in Data S5, and reflect our sample's profile and diversity. Focus groups to understand barriers and facilitators of HF management and the use of technology were led by a qualitative researcher (L.C.R.), with the support from a cardiologist (L.C.C.B.). The interviews were recorded and transcripted. The reports were then coded and classified into categories, and analyzed according to content analysis. 26 More details of the qualitative component of the study will be provided in future reportings.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Descriptive statistics were calculated using means and SDs for continuous variables, or frequency counts and percentages for categorical variables. Baseline participants' sociodemographic and clinical characteristics were compared by χ2 tests or Student t test, as appropriate. Primary and secondary outcomes analyses were made according to the “intention‐to‐treat” principle. The relative risk (RR) for the primary and secondary outcomes comparing the intervention group with the control group was calculated in R using the epiR package. 27 This package includes functions for computing the RR and its 95% CI directly from contingency table data. The 95% CI for the RR was calculated using the Wald method, and statistical significance was evaluated with the χ2 test. 27 Statistical significance was assessed with the χ2 test. The time‐to‐event analyses were done on a time‐to‐first event basis. Survival curves for time free of hospitalizations or the composite outcome of all‐cause deaths and hospitalizations were constructed according to the Kaplan‐Meier method, and the differences between curves were examined by the log‐rank statistics. As a sensitivity analysis, we compared the groups according to “per‐protocol” principle using the same statistical approach. Additionally, we evaluated the occurrence of the primary outcome for prespecified subgroups, including sex, age (stratified at 60 years), educational level (stratified at 4 years), HF cause (ischemic versus others), NYHA class II versus III and IV, and left ventricular ejection fraction (stratified at ≤50%), and calculated the P value for interaction for each subgroup. Level of significance was set at 2‐sided P<0.05. No adjustments for multiple comparisons were performed because we have considered subgroup and sensitivity analyses as hypothesis generating. All the statistical analyses were performed after database lock in March 2023 (Data S6), using R software, version 4.0.3 (https://www.r‐project.org/).

sec.title: Participant Flow Diagram and Baseline Characteristics
sec.p: Figure 1 shows the flowchart of enrollment, randomization, and follow‐up. Of the 924 screened participants, 629 were not eligible (lived outside Belo Horizonte metropolitan region [n=116], no diuretics use [n=105], on dialysis [n=37], life expectancy <6 months for other reason [n=67], dementia [n=108], illiterate [n=50], alcohol or drug abuse [n=47], planned invasive procedure in 30 days [n=44], included in other HF trial [n=13], and on respiratory isolation [n=42]), 98 refused to participate (sociodemographic characteristics in Table S1), and 70 were not included because of logistics, mainly related to the COVID‐19 pandemic. Of the 127 randomized individuals, 70 were assigned to intervention; however, 17 participants did not attend the first visit with case manager, and as such, did not receive the intervention, but had their outcomes collected through administrative databases, as prespecified in the protocol. Another 7 participants withdrew consent, but authorized contact to collect outcomes. From the 57 participants assigned to control, there were no loss to follow‐up or consent withdrawal. Recruitment was delayed from June 2021 to September 2021 because of the COVID‐19 pandemic, and extended until June 2022 to increase enrollment (Data S7). Follow‐up ended in December 2022.

Baseline characteristics of study participants were balanced between groups (Table 1). Mean±SD age was 63.6±10.7 years, 48% were women, 71% self‐reported their race as Black, and 33% had <4 years of education. For clinical characteristics, 68% had ejection fraction (EF) ≤50%, 65% of patients were in NYHA class III/IV, and 65% had >1 hospitalization in the preceding year. HF causes are shown in Table S2. GDMT for participants with EF ≤50% was also balanced between groups (Table S3).

sec.title: Primary Outcome
sec.p: HF‐related hospitalizations occurred in 18 (26%) participants of the intervention and 26 (46%) participants from the control group (RR=0.56 [95% CI, 0.35–0.92]; P<0.02) (Table 2). All rehospitalizations were primarily attributable to HF, except 1 that was attributable to a head trauma, after a cardiac‐related syncope. Time‐to‐event analysis also shows a significant higher survival free of hospitalizations in the intervention group (log‐rank test P=0.03). Kaplan‐Meier curve for the primary outcome is shown in Figure 2A.

sec.title: Secondary Outcomes
sec.p: All‐cause hospitalizations (RR=0.59 [95% CI, 0.36–0.95]; P=0.03) and the composite outcome of all‐cause deaths or hospitalizations were also reduced in the intervention (RR=0.63 [95% CI, 0.40–0.99]; P=0.04) compared with the control group (Table 2). However, Kaplan‐Meier curve shows no difference in time free of all‐cause deaths or hospitalizations between groups (log‐rank test P=0.07) (Figure 2B). For all‐cause deaths (all cardiovascular, except 1 in the intervention group attributable to COVID‐19), no difference between groups was observed.

sec.title: Prespecified Sensitivity Analyses
sec.p: Per‐protocol analysis to evaluate the effect of TMI in participants who received the intervention during 180 days (n=46) versus those in the control group shows that the results were similar, with greater effect sizes (Table S4).
Subgroup analysis also shows consistent results across different participants' profile according to age, sex, NYHA class, and ejection fraction (P‐interaction >0.05 for all subgroups) (Figure 3).

sec.title: Exploratory Analysis
sec.p: To better understand how the TMI reduced adverse outcomes, we explored the frequency of diuretic dose‐adjusting protocol activation in the intervention group, and observed that the protocol was activated 37 times, in 19 (27%) participants. There were 15 teleconsultations with the cardiologist because of alarm signs, 13 of them leading to medication change and 2 to an indication for urgent in‐person evaluation. The prespecified evaluation of participants who sought emergency care was made in the per‐protocol analysis, as it was not available in the administrative database, and revealed that 5 (11%) of the intervention group versus 17 (30%) in the control group sought emergency care. GDMT for participants with EF ≤50% was more optimized in the intervention group, particularly for angiotensin‐converting enzyme inhibitors/angiotensin receptor blockers/angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitors and β‐blockers (Table S3), but with >50% of patients still below target dose.

sec.title: Qualitative Analysis of Focus Groups
sec.p: In summary, the qualitative phase pointed out that the main barriers to HF management were lack of knowledge about HF and self‐care, and reduced access to care. The participants from the intervention group revealed that the intervention was well accepted, with the assignment of a case manager, and the channel for questions being the 2 components most cited as helpful and able to build safety, even reducing the demand for emergency care, as supported by our exploratory analysis. Interestingly, the qualitative component showed a clear distinction in HF and self‐care knowledge between groups, with the control group having less knowledge.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: In this randomized clinical trial, a multifaceted TMI consisting of an STS protocol by a nurse manager and a remote educational program significantly reduced rehospitalizations at 6 months in patients admitted because of HF and discharged from Brazilian public health system's hospitals compared with usual care. Rehospitalization rates for patients with HF declined 44% in the intervention group, from 46% to 26%, revealing relevant clinical and public health implications. The reduction in adverse outcomes was consistent for secondary outcomes, and in the sensitivity analysis, and is likely explained by on‐time adjusting of diuretics dosing, early identification of alarm signs, and better patient knowledge about HF and self‐care. Despite all the efforts to optimize GDMT in both groups, further improvement might be needed. Taken together, our study suggests that even for more vulnerable populations, TMI is an effective strategy to improve HF care during the hospital to home transition.

Although a recent meta‐analysis investigating the benefits of telemonitoring on deaths and rehospitalizations has shown a decrease in unfavorable outcomes, and encouraged TMI integration in HF care, 14 large trials that addressed the addition of TMI to HF usual care has shown conflicting results. 28 , 29 , 30 This heterogeneity may be attributable to the TMI modality (STS versus mobile applications), patient population (socioeconomic status; outpatient versus being discharged from hospital), and quality of usual care. 14 , 28 In LMICs, where literacy, income, and access to GDMT, technology, and health professionals, particularly cardiologists, may further impair HF care, TMI effects have been less investigated. 4 , 16 , 17 In fact, although some of the cited aspects may be barriers to TMI implementation in LMICs, they can be conversely seen as opportunities for TMI to complement usual care in these settings, if the clinical and public health benefits are proven in the LMIC context. As such, the present study advances knowledge in the field by showing a significant effect of TMI in reducing HF rehospitalizations in the Brazilian public health system, which has patients with low socioeconomic status, as shown by the baseline characteristic of participants.

Among the mechanisms by which the TMI reduced rehospitalizations, timely diuretic dose adjustments based on weight gain and worsening congestive symptoms should be mentioned, as they were required by more than a quarter of the participants in the intervention group. Indeed, previous studies have shown that 90% of HF hospitalizations are in the “wet and warm” profile and that 50% of patients required diuretic adjustments in the 4 to 8 weeks after hospital discharge. 31 , 32 Access to a channel for questions in working hours and to rapid teleconsultations for alarm signs might have also played a role, reducing participants from the intervention group to seek for emergent care, and consequently reducing hospitalizations. 27 Last, better acquired knowledge about HF and self‐care might have been another mechanism corroborated by the qualitative analysis. Previous studies have shown that empowering patients to enhance their engagement in care is an effective strategy to improve HF management. 12 , 33 Interestingly, our intervention was effective for the broad range of EF profiles, what may be appealing to HF with preserved EF, which has less proved evidence‐based interventions that effectively reduce subsequent hospitalizations. 34 , 35

Our results must be interpreted in the light of the study's limitations. First, calculated sample size was not achieved. Lower enrollment rate had multifactorial causes, led by the impact of COVID‐19 pandemic that resulted in the following: (1) a reduction of HF hospitalizations along with an increase in in‐hospital mortality, 19 , 36 (2) impaired access to hospitals or wards during part of the study's enrollment period, (3) a change in hospital's profiles, and (4) delayed enrollment, from May 2021 to September 2021, resulting in the loss of winter months in our enrollment period, when the incidence of HF hospitalizations is higher. 37 Moreover, refusal rate was higher than expected based on previous experiences, 38 and the digital divide must be considered a reason. 16 , 27 In fact, patients who refused to participate were more often older and less educated than those who accepted. Further analysis is necessary to understand the impact of the digital divide in the Brazilian context. Importantly, our effect size was greater than anticipated, and consistent across outcomes and sensitivity and subgroup analyses, suggesting a real benefit of TMI, although the smaller than planned sample size increases the likelihood that the observed benefit was because of chance. Second, we acknowledge some participants assigned to intervention did not receive it, as they did not attend the first and only on‐site visit. Importantly, the study results using an on‐treatment analysis showed similar and consistent findings. Third, GDMT optimization was not the focus of our nurse‐led intervention. Although the importance of optimized GDMT to reduce adverse events must be emphasized among health care professionals and patients, we anticipate that the TMI benefit might have been even higher if GDMT was more intensively optimized. Last, although our study population is socioeconomically vulnerable, it might not be representative of the all Brazilian population, as it is from an urban center of the more developed region in the country. However, access to HF care may be even more restricted in remote areas, where TMI might be an appealing option to improve HF care.

The increasing prevalence of HF in LMICs because of population aging and the improvement in care of cardiovascular conditions require innovative implementation strategies tailored to context, but prone to adaptations, to confront this scenario where prognosis is worse. 39 , 40 Our study findings suggest that an effective TMI can be tailored, and developed in a low‐resource setting. Although the COVID‐19 pandemic brought many challenges to our study logistics, it also enhanced the importance of developing alternative models to complement HF care.

sec.title: CONCLUSIONS
sec.p: A TMI reduced HF‐related rehospitalizations compared with usual care in patients hospitalized because of HF and discharged from hospitals in the Brazilian public health system. Our findings highlight the importance of digital health strategies for the management and improvement in clinical outcomes of this high‐risk population.
